newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Experts vest little faith in UK polls.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Experts vest little faith in UK polls.

text.p: A lack of faith in opinion polls after they got the result of the 1992 British election disastrously wrong has prompted many leading election experts to tone down their forecasts for Thursday's result.

A majority of opinion polls in recent weeks has predicted a landslide Labour majority of more than 200 seats. Yet the mean of expert forecasts from the latest Reuters survey of top psephologists, published on Wednesday, is 92 seats.
Fourteen out of the 20 panellists said they believed the opinion polls were overestimating the size of Labour's expected majority, making the same mistake as they did five years ago.

"I think the polls are broadly right and Labour will win," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester. "But the panel is being sensible...even the polls carried out the day before the last election were wrong."
In April 1992, the Conservatives won a fourth term with a 21-seat majority, even though most opinion polls had consistently forecast a Labour victory.

Differing degrees of faith in opinion polls were cited as the major reason for a wide range of forecasts within the Reuters survey. The highest prediction was for Labour to win a 153-seat majority, while one forecaster saw no overall majority for either of the two main parties.
"We are in a volatile position. Some people believe in the polls and others do not give them much credence," said David Denver, lecturer in politics at the University of Lancaster.
"Polls only tell us the state of play now, we are all making predictions for a future date."
Another reason for the wide range of forecasts given by Ivor Crewe, vice-chancellor at the University of Essex, is the method used to translate the percentage of votes won into parliamentary seats.
"There is no certain way to predict relationships between votes and seats and some academics place more reliance on personal instincts and hopes than they do on the polling evidence," he said.
Sydney Elliot, lecturer at Queen's University in Belfast, said he does not believe Labour will win the 50 percent support suggested by some opinion polls.
He, along with others on the panel, believes many wavering and closet Conservative voters will return to the fold at the eleventh hour and disprove opinion polls again.
"It would appear that voting Conservative has become a furtive act," said Benyon.
Colin Rallings, professor of politics at the University of Plymouth, believes opinion polls do not tell the whole story because British society in the last 10 years has become more private.
"The people who won't have anything to do with pollsters are a growing proportion of the population. They do not necessarily hold the same views as those who do talk to pollsters."
Most of the panel also expect more Conservative supporters than Labour supporters to vote on Thursday, narrowing the gap between the actual result and the predicted outcome.

"It is well established that non-voting is more prominent amongst the poor, the young and ethnic minorities. If asked on the street, these people would say they are going to vote Labour," said Denver.
